newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Talks set on Serb television channel after clashes.
newsitem.headline: Talks set on Serb television channel after clashes.

text.p: Officials from a regional TV station were due in Belgrade for talks on Friday following bloody clashes in their city over the refusal of Serbia's ruling Socialists to give up control of the station to the opposition.

Thursday's confrontation in Kragujevac, in which riot police clubbed demonstrators blockading a highway in the city south of Belgrade, beating one member of parliament unconscious, was the most violent in two months of pro-democracy demonstrations.

Vidosav Stevanovic, named director of Kragujevac's regional television station when an opposition city council took over, said he and new Mayor Veroljub Stevanovic would meet Dragoljub Milanovic, general director of state Radio Television Serbia.

Afterwards they planned to tell a rally in Kragujevac the results of their negotiations over control of the regional channel, which the dominant Socialists (SPS) refused to yield when the opposition won the city council in November.
Following the clashes, city officials in Kragujevac tried to calm tempers and urged people not to provoke incidents which could lead to further confrontations with police.

The opposition Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition, whose candidates won in Kragujevac in November, said it had offered to end the protests if two officials it has nominated to manage the regional station, RTK, were allowed to run it pending an expected court ruling on February 3.

The courts will rule on a last-minute measure passed by Kragujevac's former SPS-controlled city council integrating RTK into the national Serbian television network which is tightly controlled by the Socialists.

The independent Vienna-based International Press Institute (IPI), in an open letter to Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, condemned the police occupation of RTK and state interference in the media.
"We strongly urge you to...relinquish control of the broadcasting station immediately and allow the media to operate without further interference," the letter said.
It also deplored the brief detention of two television cameramen filming the demonstration for Associated Press, and the confiscation of their videotapes.
The Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) offered on Thursday to broker talks between the Serbian government and opposition to try to break the deadlock over the election results.

Niels Helveg Petersen of Denmark said a meeting of the Swiss, Danish and Polish foreign ministers -- the so-called troika of past, present and future OSCE chairmen -- agreed on action to try to end the impasse.
"We will insist that the Belgrade government...accept the results of the municipal elections last November," the Danish foreign minister said.

The dispute in Kragujevac was the bloodiest flashpoint in more than two months of protests across Serbia to force the Socialists to respect results of November municipal elections annulled by the government for alleged "irregularities".

Zajedno candidates won majorities on city councils in 14 cities, including Belgrade, but have been barred from taking office by a series of court rulings and government inquiries that Western countries say are designed to deliberately confuse and complicate the situation.
The protesters, into their 68th day of demonstrations across Serbia, show no signs of giving up.

Student organisers in Belgrade said they would bring lumps of earth from the 13 other towns where Zajedno results were annulled, place them in front of the police cordon and bless them with the words: "We shall not let this earth be taken away."
